questions.stem: The tissue that conducts manufactured food from the leaves to the rest of a flowering plant is the

options.text: xylem
phloem
cambium
cortex

questions.explanation: Phloem sieve tubes translocate sucrose and amino acids away from the leaves, where they are made, to any part that needs them, including roots, fruits and growing buds. Because food may be needed above or below the leaves, translocation goes in both directions.

distractorRationale.a: Xylem carries water and mineral salts, and only upwards
distractorRationale.c: Cambium is a dividing tissue that produces new xylem and phloem; it does not conduct
distractorRationale.d: The cortex is a packing and storage tissue, not a conducting tissue

questions.stem: Which feature of mature xylem vessels makes them efficient at conducting water?

options.text: They contain dense cytoplasm that pumps water along
They are dead and empty, with no end walls, forming continuous hollow tubes
Their sieve plates slow the water down so it is not lost
Their thin unlignified walls allow water to leak sideways easily

questions.explanation: A xylem vessel is a file of dead cells whose contents have broken down and whose end walls have dissolved, leaving an unbroken pipe from root to leaf. The lignin in the side walls stops the tube collapsing under the tension of the transpiration stream.

distractorRationale.a: Mature xylem has no cytoplasm at all, and water is pulled, not pumped
distractorRationale.c: Sieve plates are found in phloem, not xylem
distractorRationale.d: Xylem walls are thickened with lignin, which prevents collapse and sideways leakage

questions.stem: Water enters a root hair cell from the soil mainly by

options.text: osmosis
active transport
transpiration
capillarity through the cell wall only

questions.explanation: The cell sap of a root hair is a more concentrated solution than the dilute soil water surrounding it, so water moves across the partially permeable cell membrane from the dilute to the concentrated side. That is the definition of osmosis, and it requires no energy from the plant.

distractorRationale.b: Active transport is used for mineral salt uptake against a gradient, not for water
distractorRationale.c: Transpiration is water loss from the leaves, at the other end of the journey
distractorRationale.d: Some water does travel through cell walls, but the main entry into the cell is osmotic

questions.stem: The main force responsible for raising water to the top of a tall tree is

options.text: root pressure alone
transpiration pull, assisted by cohesion between water molecules
pumping by the cambium
active transport in the sieve tubes

questions.explanation: Evaporation from the mesophyll puts the xylem contents under tension, and because water molecules cohere strongly the whole column is dragged up as a single thread. Root pressure exists but can only push water a few metres, far short of the crown of a tall tree.

distractorRationale.a: Root pressure is real but too weak on its own to reach the top of a tall tree
distractorRationale.c: Cambium divides to form new tissue; it has no pumping function
distractorRationale.d: Sieve tubes are phloem and carry food, not the transpiration stream

questions.stem: A potted plant is moved from a dry, breezy veranda into a still, very humid room. The rate of transpiration will

options.text: increase, because the room is enclosed
decrease, because both the wind and the diffusion gradient for water vapour are reduced
stay the same, since transpiration depends only on temperature
stop completely, since stomata close in humid air

questions.explanation: Two factors change together and both slow transpiration. Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so the gradient between the leaf air spaces and the outside air is shallow, and without wind the saturated layer of air stays sitting on the leaf surface.

distractorRationale.a: Being enclosed traps moist air, which lowers rather than raises the rate
distractorRationale.c: Humidity, wind and light all affect transpiration as well as temperature
distractorRationale.d: Stomata stay open in humid air; transpiration slows but does not cease

questions.stem: Most of the water vapour lost by a leaf escapes through the

options.text: cuticle
lenticels
stomata
veins

questions.explanation: Stomata are pores in the epidermis, usually far more numerous on the lower surface, and they account for roughly ninety per cent of a leaf's water loss. A small amount does escape through the cuticle, and woody stems lose a little through lenticels, but these are minor routes.

distractorRationale.a: The waxy cuticle is designed to be waterproof; only a little water escapes through it
distractorRationale.b: Lenticels are pores in woody stems and account for a very small loss
distractorRationale.d: Veins are the vascular bundles that deliver water; they are not openings to the air

questions.stem: Translocation in the phloem can move dissolved food downwards from the leaves to the roots as well as upwards to the growing shoot.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Food travels from a source, normally a photosynthesising leaf or a storage organ that is mobilising its reserves, to any sink that needs it. Since sinks include roots below and buds and fruits above, phloem transport is two-directional, unlike the strictly upward xylem stream.

questions.stem: A ring of bark, including the phloem, is removed all the way round the trunk of a young mango tree. After some weeks the bark just above the ring swells. The best explanation is that

options.text: water from the xylem has collected there because the xylem was also cut
sugars moving down from the leaves cannot pass the gap and accumulate above it
the tree is producing extra lignin to seal the wound in the xylem
mineral salts being carried up from the roots are trapped above the ring

questions.explanation: Ringing removes the phloem but leaves the xylem, which lies deeper, intact. Water therefore still rises and the leaves keep photosynthesising, but the sugars they export can travel down only as far as the cut, so they pile up and cause the swelling. This classic experiment is the standard proof that phloem, not xylem, carries food.

distractorRationale.a: The xylem lies inside the ring of bark and is not removed by ringing
distractorRationale.c: Swelling is caused by accumulated food and new tissue growth, not by lignin sealing xylem
distractorRationale.d: Mineral salts travel in the xylem, which is undamaged, so they pass the ring freely

questions.stem: Name the process by which a plant loses water vapour from its leaves through the stomata.
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from the mesophyll surfaces followed by diffusion of the vapour out through the stomata. Do not confuse it with guttation, which is the loss of liquid droplets from the leaf margin, or with translocation, which moves food in the phloem.

questions.stem: Trace the path taken by a molecule of water from the soil to the atmosphere through a flowering plant. State three factors that would increase the rate at which the plant loses water, giving a reason for each.
markingGuide: Absorbed from soil through the root hair by osmosis (1 mark)
Passes across the root cortex from cell to cell by osmosis (1 mark)
Enters the xylem vessels in the centre of the root (1 mark)
Rises as a continuous column through the xylem of root, stem and leaf, pulled by transpiration pull and held together by cohesion (2 marks)
Passes into the mesophyll cells and evaporates into the leaf air spaces (1 mark)
Diffuses out through the stomata as water vapour (1 mark)
Factor 1: higher temperature, because water molecules evaporate faster (1 mark)
Factor 2: wind or moving air, because it removes saturated air and keeps the diffusion gradient steep (1 mark)
Factor 3: bright light or low humidity, because light opens the stomata, or because dry air steepens the vapour gradient (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The path must be given in order and must name osmosis at the root, the xylem as the route up and the stomata as the exit. For the factors, a bare list earns little; each must be tied to either faster evaporation or a steeper water vapour gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air.
